source: Gick & Holyoak (1983) Schema induction and analogical transfer
finding: Theory: a schema is made by mapping two analogs and keeping the shared structure. So two analogs should help; one alone should not. The schema stays implicit inside a single example.
numbers: Part I used 1 analog (summary, verbal principle, diagram). Part II used 2 analogs. Base rate on the radiation problem with no analog: about 10%.
quote: Indeed, the schema is defined by the correspondences between two analogs.
limits: The mechanism is argued in the paper and then tested by the number-of-analogs contrast.
agent_relevance: Schema induction needs a pair. Our agent should compare at least two solved cases, not abstract from one.

source: Gick & Holyoak (1983) Schema induction and analogical transfer
finding: Exp 1 (Maier cord problem): a story analog gave a big lift. Recall instruction and summary instruction did about the same.
numbers: Pendulum solution before hint: analog groups 71% vs control 20%. Total with hint 98% vs 30%. Recall vs summary before hint 68% vs 75%, n about 25 per cell (69 subjects).
limits: Exact cell Ns were garbled in the PDF text. Subjects read the analog as a recall task, so noticing was easy to trigger.
agent_relevance: A relevant solved case can raise success sharply. The bottleneck is whether it is retrieved and applied.

source: Gick & Holyoak (1983) Schema induction and analogical transfer
finding: Exp 2: adding a verbal statement of the principle to ONE analog gave no gain. The principle alone also worked about as well.
numbers: Convergence solution, before hint / total: analog+principle 32% / 80% (N=31); analog only 29% / 79% (N=28); principle only 28% / 66% (N=29). G2(2)=2.05, p=.36 on totals.
limits: About 30 per cell, low power. All three beat the 10% base rate.
agent_relevance: A stated principle on top of one example may add nothing. Do not assume a stated principle helps by default. Test it.

source: Gick & Holyoak (1983) Schema induction and analogical transfer
finding: Exp 3: a diagram of the principle added to ONE analog gave no gain either. Diagram alone was almost never used without a hint.
numbers: Before hint / total: analog+diagram 23% / 81% (N=26); analog only 40% / 76% (N=25); diagram only 7% / 67% (N=15).
limits: Small cells. Shows knowledge was in memory but not spontaneously noticed.
agent_relevance: Knowing the principle is not the same as noticing it applies. A trigger or check is needed.

source: Gick & Holyoak (1983) Schema induction and analogical transfer
finding: Exp 4: two analogs beat one analog plus a control story. Similar vs dissimilar pair made no reliable difference.
numbers: Before hint: 2 analogs 45% vs 1 analog 21% (G2=6.35, p<.01). Total: 80% vs 53% (G2=8.36, p<.003). Two similar 39% / 79% (N=28); two dissimilar 52% / 83% (N=23); one analog+control 21% / 53% (N=47). Total N=98.
quote: It was clearly the case that two analogs were better than one.
limits: Dissimilar pairs trended better (52 vs 39%) but not significant.
agent_relevance: Core number for the agent: two cases roughly double unaided transfer (21% to 45%) versus one case.

source: Gick & Holyoak (1983) Schema induction and analogical transfer
finding: Quality of the written schema predicted transfer. Authors of good schemas almost always solved the transfer task unaided.
numbers: Exp 4 (N=30 scored): good schema 91% before hint (10/11); intermediate 40% before hint, 90% total; poor 30% before hint, 70% total. Mix: 21% good, 20% intermediate, 59% poor. G2(4)=15.8, p<.005.
limits: Correlational: skilled solvers may write good schemas and also transfer well. Most people (59%) wrote poor schemas.
agent_relevance: Most comparisons yield weak abstractions. The agent should check the induced schema (does it name the shared mechanism?) before using it.

source: Gick & Holyoak (1983) Schema induction and analogical transfer
finding: Exp 5: with TWO analogs, a stated principle now helped, unlike with one. It raised schema quality.
numbers: Before hint: with principle 62% vs without 40% (G2=6.75, p<.01). Total 82% vs 67% (p<.05). Good schemas 44% vs 10%. N=143.
limits: Schema quality scored by hand. The with-1 vs with-2 interaction is across experiments, not one design.
agent_relevance: The principle works as a label for a schema built from two cases, not as a replacement for the cases.

source: Gick & Holyoak (1983) Schema induction and analogical transfer
finding: Exp 6: diagrams added to two analogs also helped (they had not with one). Highest transfer in the series.
numbers: Before hint / total: similar+diagram 61% / 94% (N=48); dissimilar+diagram 53% / 90% (N=51); similar no diagram 40% / 79% (N=43); dissimilar no diagram 34% / 79% (N=47). Diagram 57% vs 37% before hint (G2=7.55). Good schemas 55% vs 28%.
limits: Near ceiling (92% total with diagrams).
agent_relevance: Abstraction aids work when attached to a comparison. Scaffold: compare two cases, then state and depict the shared structure.

source: Catrambone & Holyoak (1989) Overcoming contextual limitations on problem-solving transfer
finding: Exp 1 replicated Gick and Holyoak: an instruction to compare two analogs raised unaided transfer. Comparison with one analog plus a control did not.
numbers: Before hint: 2 analogs + compare 47% (n=19) vs 16% no comparison. One analog + control 16% (n=19). Total 2 analogs 71% vs 41% for 1 analog (G2=7.16, p<.01). Two-analog compare beat the 10% base rate (G2=17.3).
limits: Small groups, about 19 each. No delay, same session and context.
agent_relevance: Comparison must be demanded, and it must be between two real analogs.

source: Catrambone & Holyoak (1989) Overcoming contextual limitations on problem-solving transfer
finding: Boundary condition: unaided transfer vanished with a 30-minute filled delay or a context shift.
numbers: Exp 2: no condition beat the 10% base rate before hint. Total with hint: 30-min delay 65% vs 1-week 42%. Comparison effect not significant at either delay. 1-week before-hint 0% (n=15).
quote: Little or no analogical transfer is obtained after a delay of even 30 min.
limits: Subjects treated the next task as unrelated. The memory existed; the cue was not used.
agent_relevance: A learned schema does not fire unless the new problem cues it. The agent needs explicit retrieval of stored schemas.

source: Catrambone & Holyoak (1989) Overcoming contextual limitations on problem-solving transfer
finding: Delayed transfer was rescued by directive comparison questions, a third example, and wording the target to match the shared structure.
numbers: Exp 4 (N=90): directive instructions 36% vs less directive 10% before hint; total 70% vs 42%. Intensity wording 32% vs dosage wording 14% before hint (p<.07). Exp 5 (1-week delay, 3 analogs, directive questions): 74% unaided overall, vs 7% and 23% in Exp 2 and 3.
limits: Question detail, third example and wording were partly confounded.
agent_relevance: Three cases plus guided questions about the key structure beat two cases with a loose prompt. Question design matters as much as count.

source: Catrambone & Holyoak (1989) Overcoming contextual limitations on problem-solving transfer
finding: Schema quality correlated with transfer, but weakly in these small samples.
numbers: Exp 1: appropriate schema 58% vs poor 29% before hint (p=.20); totals 67% vs 71% (no difference). Exp 4: appropriate schemas 32% vs 12% before hint; 68% vs 39% total (p<.02).
limits: Good schemas were rare so good and intermediate were merged. Correlation only.
agent_relevance: Do not treat a written abstraction as proof of understanding. Verify by use on a new case.

source: Thompson, Gentner & Loewenstein (2000) Avoiding missed opportunities in managerial life
finding: Masters of management students compared two cases and derived a principle. They then used it in a live negotiation far more than students who gave advice on each case.
numbers: Contingency contracts: Comparison 14/22 dyads (64%) vs Advice 5/22 (23%), chi2(1,N=44)=7.50, p<.01.
quote: Not a single person in the Advice condition drew a parallel between the two cases.
limits: The two conditions also differed in the task (derive a principle vs advise). Dyad counts are small.
agent_relevance: Per-case work does not abstract. The program should force a cross-case comparison step.

source: Thompson, Gentner & Loewenstein (2000) Avoiding missed opportunities in managerial life
finding: Quality of the principle written predicted transfer. Quality of case-by-case advice did not.
numbers: If both dyad members stated a sophisticated principle, contracts 88%; one member 45%. In Advice, good advice vs not: 2/8 (25%) vs 2/11 (18%). Coding reliability 82% to 87%.
limits: Very small counts.
agent_relevance: Grade the abstraction, not the answer to each case.

source: Thompson, Gentner & Loewenstein (2000) Avoiding missed opportunities in managerial life
finding: Cites earlier work: compare-only instruction beat advice, and naming the principle in training added nothing.
numbers: Compare 54% vs advice 13% of dyads transferred. Managers who compared were three times as likely to use contingency contracts. Mentioning the principle: no effect (Loewenstein, Thompson & Gentner 1999, cited here only).
quote: Mentioning the principle during training had no effect.
limits: Secondhand: the 1999 paper itself was not opened.
agent_relevance: The comparison act is the active ingredient, not naming the principle.

source: Gentner, Loewenstein & Thompson (2003) Learning and transfer: a general role for analogical encoding
finding: Exp 1: guided analogy training transferred a negotiation schema to a new case. Baseline did not.
numbers: Guided analogy 47% (15/32) used the trained principle in the test negotiation vs 6% baseline, chi2(1,N=48)=7.92, p<.01. Of contingent-contract trainees 44% proposed contingent contracts; 1 of 16 trade-off trainees did.
limits: Undergraduates. Transfer is to a related negotiation, not a far domain.
agent_relevance: Schema learning from two worked cases is real and specific to the principle taught.

source: Gentner, Loewenstein & Thompson (2003) Learning and transfer: a general role for analogical encoding
finding: Exp 2: comparing two cases beat studying them separately, with the same cases on the page.
numbers: Transfer: comparison 48% vs separate 19%, chi2(1,N=128)=11.85, p<.01. Fully stated schema 42% vs 13%. Linked case 2 to case 1 in 98% vs 16% (chi2=89.55). N=128, 2x2 design.
limits: Still under half transferred.
agent_relevance: A forced compare step is cheap and gives about 2.5 times the transfer rate in humans.

source: Gentner, Loewenstein & Thompson (2003) Learning and transfer: a general role for analogical encoding
finding: Exp 3: more comparison support gave more transfer in a live face-to-face negotiation.
numbers: Reported contingent-contract rates: guided analogy 90%, comparison 70%, separate cases 55%, baseline 37%. N=158 (40, 40, 40, 38). Guided = definition plus diagrams plus guiding questions.
limits: Baseline forms contracts 37% of the time anyway, so the gain over chance is smaller than it looks.
agent_relevance: A dose ladder: separate < compare < compare with a structure scaffold. Build the scaffold level, not just the compare step.

source: Loewenstein, Thompson & Gentner (2003) Analogical learning in negotiation teams
finding: Comparison training transferred in teams and solo. Teams did no better than solo individuals.
numbers: Contingent contracts: Comparison 24/60 (40%) vs Separate cases 8/37 (22%) vs Baseline 50/213 (23%); chi2(2,N=310)=7.08, p<.05. Teams 32% (12/38) vs solo 34% (20/59). Comparison vs separate alone p=.06. Mean joint gain $4.76M vs $4.28M vs $4.19M.
limits: Separate-case training did not beat no training.
agent_relevance: Studying cases one at a time can be worth nothing. A list of cases is not schema learning.

source: Loewenstein, Thompson & Gentner (2003) Analogical learning in negotiation teams
finding: Mechanism check: comparison made people state the schema more completely.
numbers: Schema induced: Comparison 21/38 (55%) vs separate 12/38 (32%), chi2(1,N=76)=4.34, p<.05.
limits: Blind raters coded 40% of responses.
agent_relevance: Supports the chain comparison, then schema, then transfer.

source: Alfieri, Nokes-Malach & Schunn (2013) Learning through case comparisons: a meta-analytic review
finding: Overall, case comparison beats sequential, single-case and no-comparison instruction across 57 experiments.
numbers: d=.50, 95% CI [.44,.56] over 336 tests from 57 experiments (abstract, read via OpenAlex).
limits: Abstract only; the full paper was not read.
agent_relevance: Prior for planning: a medium effect of about half a standard deviation, not a huge one.

source: Alfieri, Nokes-Malach & Schunn (2013) Learning through case comparisons: a meta-analytic review
finding: Four of 15 moderators were reliable: comparison objective, principle presentation, content, lag to test.
numbers: Finding similarities beats other objectives. Principles given after the comparison beat principles before. Perceptual content and immediate tests give larger effects.
quote: providing principles after the comparisons, using perceptual content, and testing learners immediately are all associated with greater learning
limits: Per-moderator effect sizes not read.
agent_relevance: Order of steps: compare first, then supply the principle label. Do not lead with the rule.

source: Alfieri, Nokes & Schunn (2011) Aligning the structural components across learning tasks of case comparisons (SREE abstract)
finding: Earlier report of the same project: random-effects model, 57 experiments, medium effect.
numbers: d=.60, 95% CI [.47,.72], I2=59.05% at the experiment level.
limits: Conference abstract. Later paper gives d=.50 at the test level.
agent_relevance: The estimate depends on the unit of analysis. Quote a range of .5 to .6.

source: McLure, Friedman & Forbus (2015) Extending analogical generalization with near-misses (ALIGN, built on SAGE)
finding: SAGE is the formal schema-induction model. Each new case is matched with SME. If similarity is above an assimilation threshold it is merged into a generalization; otherwise it is stored as its own case.
numbers: Sketch task (6 labels, chance 21%): ALIGN peak 77% vs prototypes (SAGE alone) 62% vs examples only 53%. Text also says prototypes and examples both 55% and ALIGN 7 points better (p<.01). Geospatial task: 60 examples, 6 classes, 10-fold CV.
limits: The PDF gives two overlapping figures for Exp 1. Small datasets.
agent_relevance: An algorithm to copy: compare a case to the library, merge if above threshold, keep separate otherwise.

source: McLure, Friedman & Forbus (2015) Extending analogical generalization with near-misses (ALIGN, built on SAGE)
finding: Near-misses (similar pairs with different labels) add discrimination that generalization alone lacks. The similarity threshold has a sweet spot.
numbers: Threshold 0.8 used. Too low: many incidental differences. Too high: generalizations small and numerous. Generalization alone did not significantly beat plain retrieval.
quote: there is a sweet spot for comparison
limits: Tested on sketches and map concepts, not on language reasoning.
agent_relevance: Compare a case also with a near failure, not only with successes. The contrast shows what the schema must exclude.

source: Zheng et al. (2023) Take a step back: evoking reasoning via abstraction in large language models
finding: Step-back prompting: ask for the high-level concept or first principle, then reason from it. Large gains on PaLM-2L, smaller on GPT-4.
numbers: MMLU Physics 66.4 to 73.2; Chemistry 70.9 to 81.8 (CoT 65.0 / 75.3). GPT-4 Physics 69.4 to 84.5 (CoT 82.9); Chemistry 80.9 to 85.6 (CoT 85.3). Llama2-70B Physics 51.9 to 64.8; Chemistry 55.7 to 66.7.
limits: Gain over GPT-4 CoT is small (physics +1.6, chemistry +0.3). Hand-written few-shot exemplars.
agent_relevance: Abstraction first helps modestly on strong models and a lot on weaker ones.

source: Zheng et al. (2023) Take a step back: evoking reasoning via abstraction in large language models
finding: Fact-heavy and multi-hop tasks: huge gain on TimeQA, modest on MuSiQue, none on StrategyQA.
numbers: TimeQA 40.7 to 66.0 (CoT 38.1), with RAG 68.7; hard split 39.1 to 61.6. SituatedQA 51.8 to 57.5 (RAG 61.0). MuSiQue 35.5 to 42.6 (CoT 38.7). StrategyQA 82.8 to 82.7 (RAG 86.4).
limits: The TimeQA gain is mostly a better retrieval query. StrategyQA shows no gain.
agent_relevance: Step-back works as a retrieval cue. Gains are largest where recalling the right principle or context is the bottleneck.

source: Zheng et al. (2023) Take a step back: evoking reasoning via abstraction in large language models
finding: Error analysis: abstraction is rarely the failing step. The reasoning after it is.
numbers: MMLU Physics: over 90% of errors occur in the Reasoning step; Principle (abstraction) errors are a small share. Step-back fixes up to about 40% of base-model errors and introduces up to 12% new ones. Robust to the number of exemplars (Fig 3).
limits: Error classes labelled on a PaLM-2L sample, not independently validated.
agent_relevance: The abstraction step is cheap and mostly right. Spend checks on the reasoning that follows it.

source: Yang et al. (2024) Buffer of Thoughts: thought-augmented reasoning with large language models
finding: Buffer of Thoughts distills a problem into key information, retrieves a stored thought template from a meta-buffer, instantiates it, and updates the buffer after each solved task.
numbers: GPT-4 accuracy %: Game of 24 82.4 (standard 3.0, CoT 11.0, ToT 74.0, Meta-prompting 67.0); Checkmate-in-One 86.4 (Meta-prompting 57.2); Geometric Shapes 93.6 (78.2); MGSM 89.2 (CoT 85.5); Word Sorting 100.0; Python Puzzles 52.4.
quote: requiring only 12% of the cost of multi-query prompting methods
limits: Authors' own runs, single reported number per cell. Template buffer may leak task-type information.
agent_relevance: Closest published match to a schema library: store abstract solution templates, retrieve, instantiate.

source: Yang et al. (2024) Buffer of Thoughts: thought-augmented reasoning with large language models
finding: Ablation: the problem-distiller matters more on hard tasks. Smaller models gain from the buffer.
numbers: Removing the distiller hurts Game of 24 and Checkmate-in-One more than MGSM or word sorting (Llama3-70B and GPT-4). Paper states BoT+Llama3-8B can approach or exceed plain Llama3-70B on some tasks.
limits: Exact ablation values are in a figure; not extracted here.
agent_relevance: Restate the problem into key constraints before retrieving a template.

source: Hong et al. (2024) Abstraction-of-Thought makes language models better reasoners
finding: Abstraction-of-Thought format: reason at an abstract level first, then concretize. Prompting alone helps. Finetuning on 348k AoT samples helps more.
numbers: BBH 3-shot prompting: pre-trained Llama-3-8B +15.1 points with AoT prompts over CoT prompts. Finetuned AoT vs CoT-finetuned: Llama-3-8B 82.5 vs 43.9; Mistral-7B 77.7 vs 51.6; Llama-2-7B 64.9 vs 41.9. 10k AoT samples beat 348k CoT samples.
limits: Finetuning is outside our no-training setting. Part of the gain may come from code execution in the format. Error analysis: 38% wrong reasoning steps.
agent_relevance: Abstract-then-concrete format prompting is a cheap partial gain. The finetuning table does not transfer to a scaffold.
